summary.lead: Official summary (Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House):

blocks.text: This bill increases the requirements the government must meet to obtain a nondisclosure order (NDO) under the Stored Communications Act (SCA).

The SCA generally prohibits providers of remote computing services or electronic communication services (providers) from disclosing stored electronic communications or records (e.g., emails) or information pertaining to customers or subscribers. However, the SCA authorizes the government seek a warrant, order, or subpoena to compel providers to disclose electronic communications or records or information pertaining to customers or subscribers during an investigation. Providers may notify customers and subscribers of the warrant, order, or subpoena unless the government obtains a court order—an NDO—that delays the notification.

This bill raises the standard the government must meet to obtain (or extend) an NDO. The bill also requires the court, before issuing an NDO, to issue a written determination that the standard was met based on specific and articulable facts, and to review the underlying warrant, order, or subpoena.

The bill requires NDOs to be narrowly tailored. It also limits their duration to 90 days for most investigations, though it permits a duration of up to one year for investigations pertaining to an offense involving child pornography or sexual exploitation of children.

Finally, the bill requires the Department of Justice to report annually on data related to NDOs, including the number of customers or subscribers targeted; applications for orders; orders granted, extended, or denied; and orders targeting members of the media or conduct related to certain protected activities.

The NDO Fairness Act makes it harder for the government to get a nondisclosure order, which is a court order that stops a company from telling a customer that the government has asked for their emails, records, or account information. Under current law, companies that store electronic communications generally cannot share that kind of information, but the government can compel them to hand it over during an investigation, and it can also ask a court to keep the company quiet about it.

The bill raises the standard the government must meet to get or extend one of these orders. Before a court can issue an order, it must put in writing that the standard was met, based on specific and articulable facts, and it must review the warrant, order, or subpoena behind the request. Any order must also be narrowly tailored.

Most nondisclosure orders would be limited to 90 days. The exception is investigations into offenses involving child pornography or the sexual exploitation of children, where an order may last up to one year.

The bill also requires the Department of Justice to publish a report each year on how these orders are used. The report must include the number of customers or subscribers targeted, the number of applications, and how many orders were granted, extended, or denied. It must also cover orders aimed at members of the media or at certain protected activities.
